Post-Operative Activity Guidelines Following Total Knee Replacement

Returning to normal activities after total knee replacement is a gradual process that must be guided by your recovery progress and your surgeon's clearance. This document provides a general activity progression timeline. Your individual timeline may differ based on your personal recovery.

Weeks 1–2: Limited Home Activities
During the first two weeks, focus on safety, wound healing, and beginning your physical therapy exercises. You may:
- Walk short distances within your home using your walker or crutches as instructed
- Perform the home exercise program provided by your physical therapist
- Sit in a supportive chair for meals and brief activities — limit sitting in low chairs or soft sofas that make it difficult to stand
- Use the restroom and shower independently with appropriate assistive equipment

You should NOT during weeks 1–2:
- Drive or operate any vehicle
- Climb stairs without supervision or assistive equipment
- Carry items that interfere with safe use of your walker
- Lift more than 5–10 pounds
- Perform any exercise beyond your prescribed PT program

Weeks 2–6: Gradual Return to Household Activities
As your strength and range of motion improve, you can gradually increase your activities:
- Walking distances: gradually increase from 100 feet to several blocks as tolerated
- Stair climbing: practice with handrail support; step up with the non-operative leg first, step down with the operative leg first
- Light household tasks: preparing simple meals, light cleaning from a seated position, managing personal hygiene independently
- Driving: typically cleared by your surgeon at the 6-week visit if the operative leg is not the driving leg and pain and strength are adequate

Weeks 6–12: Expanding Activity
By 6 weeks, most patients have progressed to a cane or are walking without an assistive device:
- Resume driving (if cleared by surgeon)
- Return to sedentary or desk work (typically cleared at 6 weeks)
- Begin water walking and swimming when the incision is fully healed
- Begin stationary cycling at low resistance if range of motion allows
- Continue formal or home physical therapy
- Avoid return to physically demanding work without surgical clearance

Months 3–6: Return to Function
- Return to light physical labor with surgical clearance
- Resume recreational activities such as golf (typically cleared at 3–4 months), hiking on level terrain, and dancing
- Avoid high-impact activities: running, jumping, contact sports, heavy lifting
- Begin low-impact fitness activities as tolerated

Beyond 6 Months:
- Most patients can return to all activities of daily living and most recreational activities by 6 months
- High-impact activities may remain restricted indefinitely depending on implant type and surgeon preference
- Discuss your specific activity goals (e.g., skiing, tennis, cycling) with your surgeon at annual reviews

Activities to Avoid Long-Term After Knee Replacement:
The following high-impact activities put excessive stress on the joint implant and may reduce its longevity:
- Running and jogging
- High-impact aerobics
- Contact sports (football, basketball, soccer)
- Heavy singles tennis
- Repetitive jumping

Low-impact activities that are generally acceptable long-term:
- Walking
- Swimming
- Cycling (stationary or outdoor on flat terrain)
- Elliptical trainer
- Golf
- Doubles tennis
- Dancing
- Hiking on level terrain

Fall Prevention:
Falls after joint replacement can be dangerous. Remove trip hazards from your home (loose rugs, cords, clutter). Install grab bars in the bathroom. Use a night light for nighttime bathroom trips. Wear supportive, well-fitting footwear. Do not rush — take your time with all movements, especially while taking pain medications.
